acceptance_criteria.criterion: The module exports a `launchApplication` function with the signature `(command: string, args: string[]) => Promise<void>`.
Calling `launchApplication` with a known-good command (e.g., `node`) resolves successfully.
Calling `launchApplication` with a non-existent command rejects with a descriptive error.
On Windows (`process.platform === 'win32'`), the spawn uses `shell: true`; on all other platforms, `shell: false`.
The spawned process is detached (`detached: true`) and uses `stdio: 'ignore'`.
The module uses relative `.js` import extensions consistent with the project's Node16 ESM convention.

comments.note: A03 — Injection (Windows shell:true path). File: src/server/app-launcher.ts, lines 23–26. On Windows, spawn is called with shell:true, which routes execution through cmd.exe. If `command` or any element of `args` is sourced from user-controlled input (e.g. an HTTP request parameter or config file value written by an untrusted party), shell metacharacters (&, |, >, ;, etc.) could be injected and executed. On non-Windows the risk is absent (shell:false). Remediation: (1) Enforce an allowlist of permitted commands at the call site(s) before invoking launchApplication; (2) if the call site already enforces an allowlist of known application commands (e.g. 'code', 'github'), document that constraint clearly; (3) consider stripping or rejecting arguments containing shell metacharacters when shell:true is active.

A04 — Insecure Design: no input validation. File: src/server/app-launcher.ts, line 21. The function accepts `command` and `args` without any validation — no empty-string guard, no allowlist, no length/character constraints. An empty `command` causes a synchronously thrown error that bypasses the descriptive Promise-based rejection wrapper (noted by QA). More critically, the absence of an allowlist means any caller can spawn any executable on the host OS. Remediation: (1) Add a guard for empty/blank `command` at the top of the Promise constructor; (2) consider accepting a restricted set of supported application identifiers resolved to known paths, rather than accepting arbitrary command strings.

A05 — Security Misconfiguration: error message information disclosure. File: src/server/app-launcher.ts, lines 40–43. The rejection error message includes the raw `command` string and the full OS error. If this error is ever propagated unfiltered to an HTTP response body or a client-facing log, it could reveal internal binary paths or system details. Remediation: Callers should catch and sanitize errors before forwarding to API responses. The module-level behavior is intentionally descriptive for developer use; no change required here, but callers must be mindful.

A09 — Security Logging & Monitoring: no audit trail for spawned processes. File: src/server/app-launcher.ts. There is no logging of which application was launched, with what arguments, at what time, or by which request context. In a server environment, this makes it difficult to detect abuse or audit activity. Remediation: Consider adding a structured log entry (info level) on successful spawn including the command name (but not sensitive args) and a request/session identifier if available from the caller's context.

No Critical or High security findings. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed. The implementation uses Node.js built-in spawn (no new third-party dependencies, A06 clear). No cryptographic operations (A02 clear). No authentication/session logic (A07 clear). No deserialization or dynamic code execution (A08 clear). No outbound URL fetching (A10 clear). The two Medium findings are design-level concerns that depend on how callers source their inputs — they do not represent direct exploitability within this module in isolation.

comments.note: src/server/app-launcher.ts — Applied empty-command guard at the top of the Promise constructor (lines 23–31). When command.trim() is falsy, rejects immediately with 'Failed to launch application: command must not be empty.' This prevents spawn() from throwing synchronously and bypassing the Promise-wrapped error handler, making rejection behaviour uniform across all invalid inputs. This fix is non-behavioral for any valid (non-empty) command — QA's validation remains fully intact. Flagged by both QA and Security Auditor; applied here to avoid a full bounce cycle for a trivial guard.

src/server/app-launcher.ts — The child.unref() call appears before the 'spawn' and 'error' event handlers are attached (line 42 vs lines 44–54). This is safe in Node.js because event emission is asynchronous, but the ordering can confuse readers into thinking the child's lifetime is fully severed before any handlers are registered. A brief inline comment explaining this ordering (e.g. 'unref() is safe here — event handlers are registered synchronously before the event loop can fire') would help future maintainers. Tier: Documentation-Forward.
